summary: Extends SRTP to allow selective encryption of RTP header extensions. SRTP authenticates RTP headers but does not encrypt them, yet header extensions can hold sensitive data that participants want kept confidential.

eli5.summary: A letter's envelope can be seen by everyone, but some notes written on it are private. This lets certain notes on the envelope be put in code.

questions: how to encrypt rtp header extensions
what is the srtp encryption mask
how are encrypted header extensions signaled in sdp
subtitle: A way to encrypt chosen RTP header extensions inside SRTP, using the same cipher as the media payload.

tldr.problem: SRTP authenticates RTP headers but does not encrypt them, yet header extensions can carry sensitive data such as per-packet sound levels.
tldr.mechanism: Selected extension elements are XORed with a header keystream derived from new keys (labels 0x06 and 0x07) and masked so only chosen element payloads change. The chosen elements are signaled in SDP with an encrypt URI.
tldr.outcome: Participants can keep specific extension values confidential while leaving others readable. The RFC also updates RFC 3711 so future SRTP transforms must say how header extensions are encrypted.

today: RFC 6904 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. It updates RFC 3711, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Encrypt Header Extensions
sections.content:
SRTP (RFC 3711) gives confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection for RTP payloads. To preserve RTP header compression efficiency, it gives only authentication and replay protection for the headers. For the standard header fields that is fine, since they reveal little beyond what an attacker could infer from packet size and timing.

Header extensions (RFC 5285) are different. Two specifications, RFC 6464 and RFC 6465, carry per-packet sound levels and say that exposing them to an eavesdropper is unacceptable in many circumstances. RFC 6904 therefore defines how to encrypt header extensions carried over SRTP, and lets a sender encrypt only a subset so that, for example, a network monitor can still read transmission time offsets.
sections.eli5: Most of what is written on the outside of a parcel is fine for everybody to see. But a few notes on it are secret, so this gives a way to scramble just those.

sections.title: Same Cipher, Separate Keys
sections.content:
The mechanism encrypts header extensions with the same cryptographic algorithms and parameters as the packet's RTP payload. Encrypted elements are carried like unencrypted ones. The one- or two-byte element header and any padding stay unencrypted, each element keeps its own identifier, and encrypted and unencrypted elements have separate identifiers.

To encrypt or decrypt, a participant uses the SRTP key derivation algorithm from Section 4.3.1 of RFC 3711 to make two new keys, with the same pseudorandom function, master key, master salt, index and key derivation rate as the payload.

  • k_he, the header encryption key: label 0x06, length n_e.
  • k_hs, the header salting key: label 0x07, length n_s.

No new authentication key is needed, because SRTP already authenticates the RTP headers, including extensions.
sections.eli5: The sender uses the same kind of lock as for the main message, but cuts a new pair of keys just for the envelope notes.

sections.title: The Encryption Mask and Keystream
sections.content:
A header extension keystream is generated for each packet with encrypted elements. The participant then builds an encryption mask with all-ones octets (0xff) over the payload of each encrypted element, and all-zero octets over unencrypted elements, element headers and padding. The mask is computed per packet, and a receiver can always work it out from the unencrypted parts and the signaled list.

The mask is ANDed with the keystream, and the result is XORed with the header extension. Encryption starts at the first RFC 5285 ID and length, not at the "defined by profile" or "length" fields. Equivalently: EncryptedHeader = (Encrypt(Key, Plaintext) AND MASK) OR (Plaintext AND (NOT MASK)), which suits implementations whose encryption module cannot be changed easily.

The SRTP authentication tag is computed over the encrypted extension, so encryption MUST happen before the tag is computed and validation MUST be done on the encrypted data. Receivers SHOULD decrypt only after validating the tag, and MUST NOT take security-relevant action on decrypted headers before then.
sections.eli5: A stencil has holes over the secret words only. Scrambling is applied through the holes, so the rest of the note stays readable.

sections.title: Existing and Future Transforms
sections.content:
For AES-CM and AES-f8 (RFC 3711), SEED-CTR (RFC 5669), and AES_192_CM and AES_256_CM (RFC 6188), the keystream is generated with the same transform and IV as the payload, but with k_he and k_hs in place of the payload keys. For SEED-CCM and SEED-GCM it uses the SEED-CTR algorithm, since their AEAD covers the header in its associated authenticated data and counter mode is believed to be of equivalent strength. For the NULL transform the keystream is all zero.

This document updates RFC 3711: the Standards Track RFC defining any new SRTP encryption transform MUST specify how it is used with header extension encryption. Following the approach above is RECOMMENDED where applicable and cryptographically adequate.

The RFC illustrates the mask with a header extension holding an encrypted SMPTE timecode (ID 1), a plaintext transmission time offset (ID 2), an encrypted audio level (ID 3) and an encrypted NTP timestamp (ID 4). Only the payload octets of IDs 1, 3 and 4 are masked with ones.
sections.eli5: The scrambling recipe stays the same for each kind of lock already in use. Anyone who invents a new lock must write down how it works for envelope notes.

sections.title: Signaling Encrypted Extensions in SDP
sections.content:
Encrypted elements are signaled in the SDP extmap attribute (from RFC 5285) using the URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:encrypt followed by the URI of the extension to encrypt and any attributes it normally takes. The RFC gives ABNF for this extension and an SDP example where an SMPTE timecode is encrypted while the transmission time offset is not.

If the extmap is a media attribute, it MUST be used only for media with SRTP-based RTP profiles. As a session attribute, at least one media in the session must use such a profile, and it MUST be ignored for other media. The encrypt URI MUST NOT be applied recursively to itself.

For backward compatibility, an endpoint that does not understand the URI ignores it. An endpoint MAY offer the same element both encrypted and unencrypted, but only when lack of confidentiality would be acceptable. An answerer that understands encryption SHOULD choose the encrypted form and mark the other inactive. Both forms MUST NOT be negotiated or sent. Users must beware of bid-down attacks, for example by integrity-protecting signaling.
sections.eli5: Before the call, each side tells the other which notes will be scrambled. A side that does not understand just ignores that part.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Header extension elements get security equivalent to SRTP payloads. The mechanism hides the content of elements, not which elements are present. With two-byte headers, zero-length elements and the appbits field are not protected, and extensions that do not use RFC 5285 cannot be protected. The RFC does not say when to use encryption; documents defining specific elements should give that guidance.

Middleboxes without the SRTP authentication keys cannot verify unencrypted extensions and MUST treat them as untrusted. Extensions cannot use different algorithms or keys than the payload, so it is not possible to encrypt an extension while leaving the payload in cleartext. Strong authentication is REQUIRED if an attacker setting easily guessed plaintext bits could meaningfully affect the system. The technique only works with keystream-based ciphers such as CTR or f8, not ECB or CBC.

IANA registered the extension URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:encrypt in the RTP Compact Header Extensions subregistry. The appendix has test vectors for key derivation and for header encryption with AES-CM.
sections.eli5: Hiding the notes does not hide that notes exist, and the secret notes are only as safe as the main message's lock.
